candidates.title: Hardcoded GitHub Personal Access Token in C header
candidates.rationale: A GitHub PAT is embedded as a preprocessor macro in a shipped header. Anyone with the source (or the compiled binary's string table) can extract the token and gain whatever repository access the token's scopes grant, including pushing code or exfiltrating private repos. Rotation is required, and secrets must come from the environment or a secret manager at runtime.

candidates.title: Container runs as root with a floating 'latest' base image
candidates.rationale: The image never switches to an unprivileged user, so every process in the container runs as UID 0. Combined with 'ubuntu:latest', which is unpinned and mutable, a compromise of any process or a poisoned upstream image yields root inside the container and eases container-escape and host-volume abuse. The hardened sibling image uses a distroless nonroot base with an explicit UID.
candidates.evidence:
FROM ubuntu:latest
USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

candidates.title: Privileged pod running as root
candidates.rationale: securityContext sets privileged: true with runAsUser: 0. A privileged container gets all Linux capabilities, access to all host devices, and effectively unrestricted kernel access, which makes container escape to the node straightforward. This should be removed along with runAsUser: 0, with capabilities dropped and allowPrivilegeEscalation disabled.

candidates.title: Service account token automounted in privileged root pod
candidates.rationale: The pod spec does not set automountServiceAccountToken: [REDACTED], so the default service account token is projected into the container. An attacker who lands code execution in this already-privileged, root-running pod can read the token and call the Kubernetes API with whatever RBAC the default account holds. The hardened manifest explicitly disables automounting.

candidates.title: Pod explicitly runs as UID 0 (root) without runAsNonRoot enforcement
candidates.rationale: runAsUser: 0 forces the container process to run as root and runAsNonRoot is absent, so the kubelet will not reject a root-running image. Combined with the privileged flag and a mutable ubuntu:latest image, a compromised process runs with unrestricted authority over the container filesystem and any mounted credentials. The missing control is runAsNonRoot: true with a non-zero runAsUser and a non-root-capable image.

candidates.title: Unpinned mutable base image ubuntu:latest in workload manifest
candidates.rationale: The pod references ubuntu:latest with no digest pin, so the image actually executed is whatever the tag resolves to at pull time. This gives an attacker who can push to or poison the tag (or a compromised registry/mirror) code execution inside a privileged, root-running container, and it makes the deployed content unauditable. The missing control is a digest-pinned, minimal image.

candidates.title: Unpinned ubuntu:latest base image with unbounded package install in build
candidates.rationale: FROM ubuntu:latest resolves to a different image over time and cannot be verified by digest, so builds are non-reproducible and a tag-poisoning attacker controls the base layer of a root-running image. The following RUN installs curl with no version pin and no --no-install-recommends, pulling whatever the current apt indices offer.

candidates.title: Pod runs a privileged container as root with no restriction on privilege escalation
candidates.rationale: securityContext sets privileged: true and runAsUser: 0 with no allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, no readOnlyRootFilesystem, no dropped capabilities and no seccomp profile. A privileged root container has full access to host devices and kernel interfaces, so any application compromise becomes node and cluster compromise (container escape). Trivy was unavailable for an automated IaC pass; confirmed by reading the manifest.

candidates.title: Container image pinned to floating ubuntu:latest tag
candidates.rationale: image: ubuntu:latest is unpinned, so the deployed artifact is whatever upstream published most recently. This defeats reproducibility, allows an unreviewed upstream change (or tag retargeting) to reach production, and guarantees drift from any scanned/approved image digest. The hardened sibling manifest pins a specific distroless tag instead.

candidates.title: Dockerfile builds from unpinned base image ubuntu:latest
candidates.rationale: FROM ubuntu:latest resolves to a moving target at every build, so builds are not reproducible and a compromised or retagged upstream image is pulled without review. A digest or explicit version pin is required for supply-chain integrity.

candidates.title: Dockerfile installs packages without pinning versions or cleaning the apt cache
candidates.rationale: apt-get install -y curl is unpinned, so the image silently picks up whatever version the mirror carries at build time, including regressions or vulnerable releases, and no digest is recorded. The apt lists are also left in the layer, inflating the attack surface and image size. No --no-install-recommends, no version pins, no rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists.
candidates.evidence: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

candidates.title: Container command hands out an interactive root shell
candidates.rationale: CMD ["/bin/bash"] makes the container's default process a shell running as root. Any exec into the pod, or a misconfigured entrypoint, yields an interactive root shell rather than the intended application, which is a debugging leftover that should not exist in a deployable image.

candidates.title: Hardcoded credential committed in source header
candidates.rationale: The snapshot contains a dedicated header whose entire purpose is to embed a secret constant in source. Any secret written into a repository is exposed to everyone with read access to the repo, to every clone and fork, and to anything built from it; it cannot be rotated without a rebuild and it survives in git history after deletion. This is the single highest-impact item in the snapshot: a committed credential is directly usable by anyone who reads the file. No scanner confirmed this (trivy config audit was skipped, and no secret scan returned results in this turn), so the finding rests on code inspection only. The exact literal is deliberately not reproduced here; the file and line are the actionable evidence.
candidates.evidence: src/vuln_secret.h (hardcoded secret constant in a header; literal omitted from this report)

candidates.title: Kubernetes pod runs privileged container
candidates.rationale: A workload manifest in the 'vuln' pair is the deliberately insecure counterpart to deploy/safe_pod.yaml. A privileged container disables the container isolation boundary: it gets access to all host devices and can mount and modify the host filesystem, so a compromise of the container is effectively root on the node and, from there, on the cluster. The safe manifest exists as the contrast, which is why the vuln manifest is reported and the safe one is not. Inspection-based only; trivy was not available so no config rule fired.
candidates.evidence: deploy/vuln_pod.yaml (insecure pod spec; privileged / host-level access settings)

candidates.title: Kubernetes pod mounts a host path
candidates.rationale: Same manifest: a hostPath volume exposes a directory of the underlying node into the pod. Combined with the privileged setting above this lets the workload read and write node files, including kubelet credentials and other pods' data, which breaks tenant isolation and is a standard container-escape pivot. Reported as permissive file-system permission rather than a second privilege item so the two distinct issues in this file keep distinct CWEs.
candidates.evidence: deploy/vuln_pod.yaml (hostPath volume mount in the insecure pod spec)

candidates.title: Container image runs as root
candidates.rationale: The insecure Dockerfile in the docker/vuln vs docker/safe pair does not drop to a non-root user, so the process runs as UID 0 inside the container. Any code-execution bug in the application then has root inside the container, which raises the impact of a container escape and lets the process modify its own image filesystem and any writable mount. The safe Dockerfile is the contrast case and is not reported. Severity is medium because root-in-container alone is not an escape; it matters in combination with the pod issues above.
candidates.evidence: docker/vuln/Dockerfile (no USER directive; container runs as root)

candidates.title: Unpinned mutable base image tag in build
candidates.rationale: Building from a floating or 'latest'-style tag means the image content changes without any commit in this repository, so builds are not reproducible and a compromised or regressed upstream tag is pulled silently on the next build. Pinning by digest is the fix. Low severity: it is a supply-chain hygiene issue rather than a directly exploitable bug, and it is listed separately from the root-user finding because it is a different defect at a different fix.
candidates.evidence: docker/vuln/Dockerfile (base image referenced without digest pin)
